Summary: The paper extends a frozen ~8M-parameter FastViT-SA24 multi-task edge perception core with small read-only plug-in modules on its stride-8 features. The core has segmentation, inverse-depth, lane and gate-corner heads. The modules are a CornerRefiner (sub-pixel corner refinement), a CornerPeakHead (confirming weak detections) and a NearGateHead (frame-filling gates), followed by two parameter-free steps: global NMS at IoU 0.2 and a 14 px minimum-box-size filter. Because the modules never write into the core, all general-task outputs are preserved exactly. The system replaces the dedicated GateNet detector in a third-party Isaac Lab drone-racing stack (learned policy + EKF). On 128 flights per arm over held-out seeds, it reaches 87.5% success versus 82.0% for GateNet. The difference is not significant (seed-level sign test p≈0.14), and the authors explicitly claim parity rather than superiority. The paper also documents a development path from 37.5% to 87.5%, with two lessons: offline crop metrics did not predict closed-loop success, and duplicate detections were catastrophic for the EKF. It reports Jetson Orin NX latency and energy for the reparameterized core (26.4 ms at 15 W).
Strengths: Unusually honest and transparent reporting. The non-significance, simulation-only scope, far-gate degradation, unmatched seed subsets in the min-size sweep and missing module latency are all stated explicitly.

Closed-loop evaluation with separated validation and final test seeds, multiple drones per seed, a seed-level sign test, Wilson intervals and an explicit loop-noise estimate. This is more rigorous than typical offline-only perception evaluation.

Practically relevant edge setting (one multi-task model on Jetson Orin NX), with concrete latency and energy measurements in two power modes. These show the importance of structural reparameterization (44.2→26.4 ms).
Negative results on core retraining are reported, which is useful for practitioners, albeit only qualitatively.
Clear writing and well-annotated figures that make the development path easy to follow.
Weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Attaching new heads to stop-gradient frozen features is standard practice (multi-head frozen trunks, probing, Side-Tuning, Ladder Side-Tuning). Exact preservation of the original outputs (Eq. 3) is a trivial identity rather than a technical contribution. The closest prior art (side-tuning-style methods) is not discussed. Framing the work against adapters, VPT and WiSE-FT is partly a straw man, since those methods deliberately adapt the shared representation.

The plug-in modules are essentially undescribed. Architectures, parameter counts, FLOPs, training data (simulator vs. real), labels, losses and schedules are missing, and the 'Step B synthesised peaks' are vague. This makes the work irreproducible and leaves unclear whether the modules are themselves application-trained on simulator data, which would weaken the contrast with the 'dedicated' GateNet.

The main closed-loop claim is statistically weak (12/5/15 seed W/L/T, p≈0.14, overlapping intervals). It rests on one simulated application and one baseline, so even the parity claim has limited generality.

The negative results on core modification (sim fine-tuning, corner loss weights 10/40/100, stride-2 head, model soups) are stated without closed-loop or general-metric numbers. The claim that modifying the core hurts other tasks without helping the target is therefore asserted rather than shown.

Seed protocol concerns. 'Clean' development seeds were evaluated after each step and plausibly informed subsequent design choices, so only seeds 141–176 are truly held out. Step-wise results with 32–64 flights lie within the stated ±10–15 point loop noise.

The real-gate offline comparison (0.987 vs 0.776 within 20 px) evaluates the core alone, not the full system with modules. It also pits a model trained on real gates against a simulator-only detector, so it neither supports real-world robustness of the modules nor constitutes a fair generalization comparison.
The 'offline metrics mislead' lesson rests mainly on a well-known EKF data-association failure (duplicate landmarks). It is not supported by a systematic offline-online correlation analysis.
Questions: What are the architectures, parameter counts, FLOPs, input features, training data (simulator, real or both), labels and losses of CornerRefiner, CornerPeakHead and NearGateHead?

What is the end-to-end latency and energy (core + modules + NMS + filter) on the Jetson Orin NX at 15 W? Does it fit the 33.3 ms budget? How does it compare with GateNet's cost and with running core + GateNet side by side?
How does GateNet perform in closed loop with the same global NMS (IoU 0.2) and 14 px minimum-size filter?
Can you provide a leave-one-module-out ablation of the final configuration on the final (or matched validation) seeds?
Can you report closed-loop success and general-metric changes for each core-modification attempt (loss weights, stride-2 head, soups, sim fine-tuning)?
How does the approach differ from side-tuning / ladder side-tuning or simply training extra heads on frozen features?
How does the full system with modules perform on the real-gate set and TII video? Was GateNet trained only on simulator data, and would training it on the same real data close the gap?
Which development seeds informed design decisions, and which seeds were never examined before the final configuration was frozen?
What causes the far-gate regression? Does a distance-aware min-size filter recover it?
Is the core's input resolution 448 or 384, and which resolution do the Table 3 metrics correspond to?
